newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Juppe responds to abuse with a book.
newsitem.headline: France's Juppe responds to abuse with a book.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe says a woman who yelled abuse at him in the street inspired him to secretly write a book, going on sale on Tuesday, to explain his unpopular policies to sceptical French citizens.
Pleading for understanding in his 116-page "Entre Nous" (Between You and Me) book, Juppe revealed a streak of joking self-deprecation that belied his image as a brilliant but cold technocrat.

Going on sale just in time for Christmas presents for fans of the least popular prime minister in modern French history, Juppe's expressed twin feelings of enthusiasm and suffering in his job. The book is from NiL publishers.
Looking uncomfortable, Juppe later denied in a television interview that he wrote the book in order to seek the affection of his compatriots.
"I would prefer to be loved than to not be loved, but I am not complaining. If I said I didn't care, people would say I was indifferent (to what they thought)," he told TF1 television.

Juppe, 51, often accused of being aloof and out-of-touch with everyday concerns, said: "I don't live outside the real world. I wanted to show in this book that I live in the same world as everyone else."
He complained he was looked at by politicians and journalists "the way that people look at a bullfight waiting for the bull to be killed".
Juppe defended his blunt style, saying: "Is politics about being a demagogue all day long? When you like people, you also have to tell them the truth."
He said in the interview and the book he expected to stay on until legislative elections in 1998. The book was released to the media on Monday.

In the book, he defended policies aimed at helping France qualify for a single European currency from 1999, saying there were no alternatives to the budget austerity that opposition parties say have aggravated record 12.6 percent unemployment.
Explaining why he wrote the book, Juppe said he was strolling one day in the streets of his southwestern city of Bordeaux when he spotted a couple walking towards him.
"Fashionable-looking. Pretty woman. They look friendly. At the moment they pass, the woman starts leaping like a goat kid. She shouts: 'Death to the bloody idiot!"'

"I was her target, there's no doubt. Pretty passer-by, I wanted to reply to you," Juppe wrote in his book, whose plain white cover patriotically uses red and blue lettering -- the colours of the French flag.

Beyond the woman, he said he hoped to be better understood by French people in hostile opinion polls, reporters who look "wide-eyed with incredulity" when he vows to stay on until 1998 and critics from his own centre-right coalition.

"The French people grumble about change and since I'm trying to force this change, they find it a relief to blame me for their ills," Juppe wrote, echoing complaints by President Jacques Chirac last week that France was too conservative.
Juppe found time to write the book between his jobs as prime minister, mayor of Bordeaux and head of the ruling Rally for the Republic (RPR) party, founded in 1976 by Chirac.
